question: Why did the authors propose the Transformer architecture, and what limitations of recurrent neural networks were they trying to address?
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: The authors sought to remove recurrence and its inherently sequential computation, which prevents parallelization across positions within a training example. The Transformer instead uses attention to connect input and output positions globally, improving parallelization and training efficiency while maintaining strong sequence-transduction quality.

question: What is self-attention, and how does it allow a model to capture relationships between different positions in an input sequence?
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: Self-attention relates different positions within the same sequence to compute each position's representation. Each position can use information from other positions in the sequence, allowing dependencies to be modeled without recurrence and regardless of their distance.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: Explain the difference between encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention and encoder-decoder attention.
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: In encoder self-attention, queries, keys and values come from the encoder's previous layer, so each input position can attend to all input positions. Decoder self-attention uses decoder representations but masks future positions, so a position attends only to itself and earlier positions. In encoder-decoder attention, queries come from the decoder while keys and values come from the encoder output, allowing each decoder position to attend across the input sequence.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: What are Query, Key and Value vectors in the scaled dot-product attention mechanism? Explain how they interact to produce the attention output.
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: An attention operation maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output. The query is compared with each key to produce compatibility scores; the scores are scaled and passed through softmax to form weights; the output is the weighted sum of the corresponding values.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: What is positional encoding, and why is it necessary in the Transformer architecture?
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: Because the Transformer has neither recurrence nor convolution, positional information must be added so it can use token order. The paper adds positional encodings to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The encodings have the same dimension as the embeddings and can therefore be summed with them.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: Explain the scaled dot-product attention equation. Why do the authors divide the query-key dot product by the square root of the key dimension?
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: The operation is Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V. Query-key dot products are divided by √dₖ before softmax. The authors explain that, for large key dimensions, dot products can become large and push softmax into regions with extremely small gradients; scaling counteracts this effect.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: How does multi-head attention differ from single-head attention? Why does the paper suggest that multiple attention heads are beneficial?
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: Multi-head attention projects queries, keys and values into multiple learned subspaces, computes attention in parallel for each head, concatenates the results and applies a final projection. It lets the model attend jointly to information from different representation subspaces and positions; a single head can lose this diversity through averaging.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: Describe the architecture of one Transformer encoder layer and one decoder layer. What are the sub-layers, residual connections and normalization operations used in each?
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: An encoder layer has multi-head self-attention followed by a position-wise feed-forward network. Each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection and followed by layer normalization, expressed as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). A decoder layer has those two sub-layers plus a third encoder-decoder attention sub-layer; its self-attention is masked to prevent attending to subsequent positions. The paper's base architecture stacks six encoder and six decoder layers.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: Why does the Transformer decoder use masked multi-head self-attention? What would happen if future positions were not masked during autoregressive generation?
paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)
expected_answer: The mask prevents a decoder position from attending to subsequent positions. Together with shifting the output embeddings, this ensures the prediction at position i depends only on known outputs before i. Without the mask, training-time predictions could use future target tokens, violating the autoregressive generation constraint and leaking information unavailable at inference.

expected_source.paper: Attention Is All You Need (arXiv:1706.03762v7)

question: According to the paper, how does the computational complexity and maximum path length of self-attention compare with recurrent and convolutional layers?

Convolutional layers have O(k·n·d²) complexity, O(1) sequential operations and O(logₖ(n)) maximum path length. The paper notes self-attention is faster than recurrent layers when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimension d.
